p.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Social Networks

ext.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Social Networks
ext.document_type: Theoretical computer science paper (conference-style; inferred from "full version due to space constraints" and the Proc. citations; the text does not state venue or year)
ext.coverage: Full text read in one pass (text lines 1-336, all of 16802 chars), including abstract, introduction, model, best-response analysis, first-mover analysis, tree FPTAS, proofs, acknowledgments and references. Some proofs (Lemma 3, Lemma 4 is given; Lemma 3 deferred) and the directed-line and arborescence extensions are stated as deferred to a full version and are not in this text.
ext.research_question: How do multiple players (companies or innovations) competing by viral word-of-mouth choose initial seed sets in a social network under a generalized independent cascade model? Specifically: best responses to an opponent's strategy, the efficiency of equilibria ("price of competition"), first-mover strategies in a two-player duopoly, and whether single-player influence maximization admits an FPTAS on bidirected trees.
ext.theory: Independent cascade model of diffusion (Goldenberg et al.; Kempe, Kleinberg, Tardos), extended to multiple competing colors. Motivated by Hotelling's model of competition and by competitive facility location and Voronoi games (text lines 47-48). Uses submodular utility systems (Vetta) and submodular maximization via greedy (Nemhauser, Wolsey, Fisher).
ext.data: None. Purely theoretical analysis; no sample, unit of analysis, time period, or N is reported.
ext.method: Formal model definition with exponentially distributed activation delays and random color tie-breaking (Section 2, lines 63-85). Best-response analysis via a deterministic equivalent of the random process and proof of monotone submodularity of expected reach (Lemma 1, Section 3). Approximation via greedy for submodular maximization. Equilibrium efficiency via Vetta's utility-system theorem (Section 3). First-mover analysis on lines via dynamic programming over a cutoff point c, with Lemma 2 (optimal solution cuts each line into equal pieces) (Section 4). FPTAS for bidirected trees via dynamic programming over subtree values G(v,k,q+,q-) with probability rounding at granularity delta = epsilon/n^3 and an inductive error bound (Theorem 3, Section 5).
ext.identification: Not applicable. No empirical identification strategy; results are worst-case approximation and proof-based guarantees.
ext.scope: Population, institution, and era: none. Scope is abstract graphs: directed graphs G=(V,E) with edge activation probabilities; two-player duopoly for first-mover results (Section 4); multi-player game for best response and price of competition; bidirected trees for the FPTAS (with the extension to bounded treewidth claimed but not shown).

key_findings.finding: Best response to fixed opponent strategies: player i's expected reach is a monotone and submodular function of S_i, so greedy gives a (1-1/e) approximation to the best response for the last player to commit.
key_findings.location: Section 3, Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 (abstract lines 15-16; intro lines 51-52; proof lines 92-120)

key_findings.finding: Price of competition (uncoordinated equilibria vs. single controller with all seeds) is at most 2, via Vetta's utility-system theorem applied to the total activated set, which is monotone submodular in the union of seeds.
Game has no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in general, but mixed-strategy Nash equilibria exist.

Two-player first-mover game on disjoint lines: the optimal solution cuts every line into equal-sized pieces, so the red player need only try n*k candidate cutoff values l_i/j (i=1..n, j=1..k), giving a strongly polynomial dynamic program.
key_findings.location: Section 4, Lemma 2 and paragraph at lines 149-153
key_findings.numbers: n*k candidate cutoff values; lines of lengths l_1..l_n; k cuts

key_findings.finding: FPTAS for single-player influence maximization on bidirected trees, including unequal probabilities in opposite edge directions: a 1-epsilon approximation, with rounding granularity delta = epsilon/n^3 and additive error at most delta*n^3 <= epsilon <= epsilon*OPT.
key_findings.location: Section 5, Theorem 3 and the closing paragraph after its proof (lines 176-231)
key_findings.numbers: delta = epsilon/n^3; approximation 1-epsilon; additive error <= epsilon*OPT

key_findings.finding: Conjecture (not proven): influence maximization is NP-complete even for arborescences directed into a root. The general problem is already known NP-complete (cited to [3,4]) and APX-hard (cited to [3]).

limitations: Several proofs are deferred to a full version because of space constraints: Lemma 3 proof, and the extensions of the first-mover line algorithm to directed lines and outdirected arborescences (lines 168-171, 299-300).
The arborescence NP-completeness result is only conjectured (lines 59-60).
The FPTAS extension to bounded-treewidth graphs is asserted with a significant increase in complexity but not shown (lines 177-178).

The game has no pure-strategy Nash equilibria in general (lines 83-85), so equilibrium results rely on mixed strategies, and the reasoning about the price of competition relies on Vetta's theorem as cited.
Footnote 1 says more realistic marketing models reduce to the model here, citing [3]; this reduction is not argued in the text (lines 40-41).
The first-mover analysis is restricted to a duopoly with two players and to disjoint or directed line structures (Section 4).
No empirical evaluation, no real network data, and no computational experiments are reported.
references_of_note: Domingos, P., Richardson, M. (2001). Mining the network value of customers. KDD. Formalized influence maximization as an optimization problem (text ref 1; lines 33-35).
Goldenberg, J., Libai, B., Muller, E. (2001). Talk of the network: word-of-mouth process. Marketing Letters. Source of the independent cascade model the paper generalizes (text ref 2; lines 46, 64).

Kempe, D., Kleinberg, J., Tardos, E. (2003). Maximizing the spread of influence in a social network. KDD. Greedy (1-1/e) guarantee for single-player influence maximization, NP-completeness (text ref 3; lines 35-36, 120, 175).
Kempe, D., Kleinberg, J., Tardos, E. (2005). Influential nodes in a diffusion model for social networks. ICALP. Provable approximation guarantees (text ref 4; lines 35-36, 58-59).
Mossel, E., Roch, S. (2007). On the submodularity of influence in social networks. STOC. Submodularity result underlying the greedy argument (text ref 5; lines 35-36).
Hotelling, H. (1929). Stability in competition. Economic Journal. The competition model the paper extends (text ref 6; lines 47-48).
Ahn, H. et al. (2001). Competitive facility location along a highway. COCOON. Related competitive facility location (text ref 7; line 48).
Cheong, O., Har-Peled, S., Linial, N., Matousek, J. (2004). The one-round Voronoi game. Related Voronoi games (text ref 8; line 48).

Nemhauser, G., Wolsey, L., Fisher, M. (1978). An analysis of the approximations for maximizing submodular set functions. Mathematical Programming. Greedy guarantee for submodular maximization (text ref 9; line 119 cites [3]).

Vetta, A. (2002). Nash equilibria in competitive societies with applications to facility location, traffic routing and auctions. FOCS. Utility-system theorem (Theorem 3.4) used for the price-of-competition bound (text ref 10; lines 122-127).

short_quotes.quote: We give a (1−1/e) approximation algorithm for computing the best response to an opponent's strategy
Our model extends Hotelling's model of competition [6], and is related to competitive facility location and Voronoi games
we conjecture it is so even for arborescences directed into a root.

rel.summary_md:
Bharathi, Kempe and Salek extend the independent cascade model so that several players compete. Each player seeds a set of nodes. Every node adopts the first colour that reaches it, activation delays are exponentially distributed, and simultaneous arrivals are broken at random. The paper proves four things. (1) If the opponent's seeds are fixed, a player's expected reach is monotone and submodular in its own seeds, so greedy seeding achieves (1-1/e) of the best response. This holds only for the last player to commit. (2) Uncoordinated equilibria lose at most a factor of 2 against a single controller of all seeds (the price of competition). (3) Pure Nash equilibria need not exist, and the first-mover problem is solved only on disjoint lines. (4) An FPTAS exists for single-player influence maximization on bidirected trees. The paper is purely theoretical: it uses no data, estimates no parameters, and reports no experiments.

The paper matters because Melange explicitly names it as the basis of its A/B coalition cascade (scenario.py:6-12). The CU colour is A and the anti colour is B, where B is the anti-tier members plus neutrals mobilized by industry money with probability min(0.9, $/400k). The system cites the paper's last-mover submodularity result to justify lazy greedy and its non-additivity reporting.

Reading the code turned up three departures. None of these points has been reproduced by a second path, so all are UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
- **Tie-breaking:** the cascade advances in synchronous hops and always processes A nodes first, so pro-CU wins every same-hop tie. The paper uses continuous random delays with random tie-breaking.
- **Frontier greedy:** the budget frontier ranks seeds by marginal spread times a leverage or competitiveness factor, not by raw marginal spread, so the clean (1-1/e) guarantee on spread does not apply. Electoral mode also removes opponent seeds, which Lemma 1 does not cover.
- **Coalition allocator:** it water-fills money in proportion to single-seed marginals and runs no greedy at all.

The paper also leaves an open question for the system: industry is modelled as a fixed opponent that never responds to CU's choices. The paper shows that once the rival best-responds, guarantees exist only for lines.

bearings.paper_claim: Multiple colours run independent cascades on a shared graph. A node adopts the first colour to reach it, with exponentially distributed activation delays and random tie-breaking among colours that arrive together. A deterministic live-edge equivalent exists in which each edge is live once, whatever colour uses it.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2, model definition (text lines 63-85); Section 3, deterministic equivalent used in Lemma 1 (lines 92-120)
bearings.system_side: The two-colour first-to-reach cascade draws one splitmix value per (iteration, edge), and that draw is the same whichever colour attempts the edge. This matches the paper's live-edge equivalent. A coloured node is never recoloured (`v not in col`). The anti colour B is the anti-tier members plus neutral bystanders drawn with probability min(0.9, industry$/400000). This is the system's own mapping of the paper's opponent seed set to industry money; the paper gives it no basis.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The structure carries over: per-edge draws, first colour wins, and the colour is permanent. The calibration does not. The paper gives no edge probabilities, no saturation constant and no money-to-seed mapping. The kernel x/(x+6) and BSCALE=400000 remain design choices, and the paper is theoretical, with no legislative data.

bearings.paper_claim: Players that reach a node simultaneously are tie-broken uniformly at random, and with continuous exponential delays simultaneous arrival is otherwise a measure-zero event.
bearings.system_side: The cascade is hop-synchronous breadth-first search. The frontier is seeded A-first: col is built from sorted A, then sorted B. Children are appended in processing order, so every A-coloured node in a layer is processed before any B node. Any neutral reached in the same hop by both colours therefore turns pro-CU, which is a deterministic tie-break in CU's favour. Same-hop ties are common under unit-hop timing.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The fact that the tie-break is fixed comes straight from the code. How much it inflates base spread and marginals is unmeasured. A check would rerun with B-first or randomized processing order under the same CRN draws and compare spreads. That remains UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). Submodularity in A probably survives, because the A-reached set with A winning ties is a union of per-seed regions, but that argument is not proven here.

bearings.paper_claim: Against a fixed opponent strategy, the last player's expected reach is monotone and submodular in its own seed set, so greedy achieves a (1-1/e) approximation of the best response.
bearings.paper_location: Section 3, Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 (lines 92-120); abstract lines 13-16
bearings.system_side: Lazy greedy picks up to 60 seeds and ranks each candidate by max(0, spread gain) x fac[c]. Here fac is the Ballotpedia leverage, or the competitiveness multiplier c when COMPET_MULT is on, and it is REPFAC x lev for contest plays. Seed activation is gated at random (Chen contingency). Electoral mode also removes anti seeds (contest) and holds at-risk allies (defend). The docstring claims the (1-1/e) bound covers the coalition side.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Lemma 1 covers raw expected spread when B is fixed and the actions are adding A seeds. Independent random seed gating preserves submodularity, since it is an expectation over independent masks. Two features fall outside the guarantee. First, ranking by a fac-weighted marginal is a cost-benefit heuristic; it is not the paper's greedy. Second, contest seeds remove B seeds, an action Lemma 1 does not cover. MC=20 noise also weakens any exact guarantee, although CRN helps. The bound therefore holds only for coalition mode with all fac=1 (LEV=0).

bearings.paper_claim: Reach is submodular in a player's own seeds (Lemma 1), so individual marginals sum to more than the joint gain. The (1-1/e) guarantee belongs to the greedy algorithm that adds seeds one at a time.
bearings.system_side: The coalition allocator computes single-seed marginals against the base state, multiplies them by (1 + 0.8 bpf), water-fills $2M with a $50k cap in proportion to those values, and then reports the honest joint spread of the funded set. Its code comment rests on the claim that spread is submodular.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports reporting a joint figure rather than a naive additive one, because submodularity implies sub-additivity. It does not give the proportional water-fill any approximation guarantee, since singleton marginals plus proportional money is not greedy. The bpf boost is likewise outside the model. Keep calling this allocator diagnostic, as it is labelled now.

bearings.paper_claim: The best-response guarantee holds only for the last player to commit. Pure Nash equilibria need not exist, and only mixed equilibria are guaranteed. The first-mover problem is solved only for a duopoly on disjoint lines (n*k candidate cutoffs). Uncoordinated competition costs at most a factor of 2 relative to one controller.
bearings.system_side: Scenarios hold industry fixed. Competitor money enters only as exogenous bystander probabilities and as the comp leg of money_response; industry never re-optimizes against CU's allocation. The docstring correctly limits the guarantee to the follower facing a fixed opponent.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The fixed-opponent framing holds only if industry commits first and does not react. FEC filings are public, so industry PACs can see CU giving and respond within a cycle. If they do, CU is the first mover on a general graph, where the paper offers no algorithm or guarantee. The price-of-competition-2 bound concerns total activations across all players, not CU's share, so it says nothing about CU's outcome.

gaps_exposed: No opponent response: industry is an exogenous bystander-mobilization rate, never a strategic seeder. Under the paper's results, CU's greedy plan is a best response only if industry has already committed and will not react. The system has no first-mover or equilibrium analysis and no sensitivity test of a reacting rival.

The tie-break is hop-synchronous with A processed first, not random, so pro-CU wins every same-hop contest. The size of this bias is unmeasured. A CRN rerun with randomized or B-first frontier order would bound it.

The cascade has no timing model. The paper's exponential delays make arrival order depend on path timing, while the system uses unit hops. That affects who wins contested neutrals and cannot be calibrated, because the system has no join-timing data.

The (1-1/e) claim in scenario.py's docstring is broader than what the code satisfies. It holds only for coalition-mode frontier greedy with fac=1. It does not hold for leverage-weighted ranking, for contest plays that remove opponent seeds, or for the proportional water-fill coalition allocator.

The paper gives no empirical calibration: no edge probabilities, no saturation constant, and no money-to-seed mapping. The bystander rule min(0.9, $/400k) and the kernel constant 6 have no source in it.
flags: The brain notes (topics/2026-06-feature-cosponsor-and-sector-networks-june-network-plan.md:80,85) and scenario.py:9-12 say the coalition side is 'Submodular, so greedy (1-1/e)'. The code departs from the paper's conditions through deterministic A-first tie-breaking, leverage-weighted marginals, contest-seed removal, and proportional allocation in per_topic_coalition. The guarantee claim should be narrowed. This finding is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
Expected spread is a heuristic model output. It is not a probability that members will join or a measure of access (D-025), and the paper has no legislative data to calibrate it.

The competitiveness multiplier enters the frontier's greedy ranking through fac. Its premise that dollars buy more in competitive seats is not validated (D-104..D-108), and the paper does not support it.
The paper proposes neither of the two rejected SNA changes (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). It does not use LDA as an edge source.
rel.paul_alignment: The paper partly agrees with Paul's takeaway. He wants rival industries modelled explicitly (his margin note on Kim et al. 2025 about conflicting industries) and cheap scenario simulation (Fink). The paper gives the formal basis for treating rival industries as a competing colour, and the built Monte Carlo with common random numbers is a faithful live-edge implementation of the model. But Paul's notes treat competitive influence maximization as solved by greedy. The paper says greedy works only when the rival has already moved and will not react. If the rival responds, no pure equilibrium is guaranteed, and the first-mover problem is solved only on lines. Paul's position on this component should therefore record two caveats: industry is never strategic in the build, and the cascade breaks every tie in CU's favour. His Chen 2023 note that high-ranking pressure is 'not diminishing' challenges submodularity under linear-threshold contagion. It does not undercut the independent cascade result here, which is the regime Lemma 1 covers.

related.why: This is the competitive linear-threshold counterpart, in which submodularity can fail. The system cites it for the FLIP channel and cites Bharathi for the coalition cascade (scenario.py:9-12).
It adds random seed take-up, which the frontier and coalition allocators layer on top of the Bharathi cascade through gate(n). Independent take-up preserves Lemma 1's submodularity.
It supplies the adaptive and lazy-greedy guarantee scope that optimize.py uses alongside Bharathi's static best-response bound.
It studies competitive influence maximization with explicit timing and network heterogeneity, the timing dimension that the hop-synchronous cascade drops.
It offers competitive heuristics under voting dynamics and is the cited basis of the contested-bills counterparty term, an alternative to independent-cascade competition.
It also uses single-player independent cascade influence maximization, and the June plan named it as the centrality-heuristic seeding companion to Bharathi.
